title: Click, Clue, Escape: making copyright training an adventure
content:
Erica Levi is the copyright lead at Lanchester Library, Coventry University. This is the second in a series of posts from her. Her team specialises in embedding Open Educational Resources in teaching at the university.  She advises and trains colleagues on copyright and licences. Since copyright still seems like a dreary topic for most colleagues, Erica sets herself a mission to develop online educational games. She writes…..

I have come to recognise a reaction when I tell people my job involves copyright: the familiar glazing over of the eyes.

That has always bothered me. Advocating for copyright and helping colleagues engage with it are important parts of my role. But how do you make copyright interesting?

A straightforward training session can easily become a long list of dos and don’ts, and lists do not necessarily inspire. So, I started experimenting with something different: storytelling through games.

From telling to doing

Stories help us make sense of information and encourage us to care about what happens next. Games take this a step further by asking us to do something.

Combine the two, and the learner can become the protagonist.

title: A copyright advent calendar – making copyright literacy a little more playful
content:
Erica Levi is the he copyright lead at Lanchester Library, Coventry University. Her team specialises in embedding Open Educational Resources in teaching at the university.  She advises and train colleagues on copyright and licences. Since copyright still seems like a dreary topic for most colleagues, she set herself a mission to develop online educational games. She tell us….

When Halloween decorations appear in shops before we have quite accepted that summer is over, and Christmas merchandise follows closely behind, my thoughts inevitably turn to how to bring copyright into it. Perhaps that is an occupational hazard?

But there is a serious idea behind it. Over the years, I have become increasingly interested in how we can make copyright education feel less daunting and more inviting. Copyright is important, but that doesn’t mean learning about it always has to involve lengthy guidance, formal training, or lots of text. Sometimes a quiz, a game or a slightly silly seasonal scenario can start a conversation just as effectively.

Certain times of year also give us a ready-made excuse to try something different. I like to latch onto calendar events, really. 

Why make copyright seasonal?
